title: G. K. Chesterton Statue in Ponchatoula
description: A larger-than-life statue of G. K. Chesterton stands at Chesterton Square in Ponchatoula. The square was reported complete in June 2009.
subtitle: Larger-than-life bronze at Chesterton Square
lede: Chesterton Square in Ponchatoula was reported complete in June 2009, with a larger-than-life statue of G. K. Chesterton and the motto "A Place to Celebrate Life."
paragraphs: On June 26, 2009, the American Chesterton Society blog said the statue and Chesterton Square in Louisiana were complete. The post called the figure larger than life and quoted the square's motto, "A Place to Celebrate Life." A commenter living near Ponchatoula said a visit was planned, and the blog pointed readers to chestertonsquare.com.

A May 28, 2008, post on the same blog quoted a Times report on the statue before it went up. That account said Dr. Bob Benson asked Milwaukee sculptor David Wanner for a full-size cast bronze, about 7 feet tall and nearly 600 pounds, on a 3- to 4-foot pedestal at the railroad-avenue entrance to the Chesterton Centre. Benson wanted Chesterton to look as if he had fallen asleep on the train and stepped off in Ponchatoula. Those figures are the pre-installation description, not a later measurement.

NOLA.com adds the local nickname Touchdown Jesus, a French inscription reading "Sacred Heart of Jesus, I have confidence in you," and a carving from the Lenzi studio in Pietrasanta, Italy.

Archbishop Gregory Aymond's August 29, 2015, homily said tree limbs took three fingers from Jesus' left hand, that cleanup crews found one finger, and that Archbishop Alfred Hughes spoke of the missing fingers at a homecoming Mass on October 2, 2005. The fingers stayed off for ten years. name: Statue of Louis Armstrong

description: Elizabeth Catlett's bronze of Louis Armstrong, with trumpet and handkerchief, was unveiled in Armstrong Park on April 15, 1980.

paragraphs: Gambit Weekly says fundraising for a statue of Louis Armstrong began in 1969 and intensified after his death in 1971. Jazz historian Floyd Levin credited Danny Barker with the idea. Elizabeth Catlett, who had chaired the art department at Dillard University in the 1940s, cast the bronze in Mexico. Gambit calls it a one-ton, 11-foot statue that cost $30,000. It was unveiled in Jackson Square on July 4, 1976, a date then believed to be Armstrong's birthday. Later research put his birth on August 4, 1901. The trumpet was damaged in shipping and repaired in time by Lin Emery, A. W. Klein, and Gerold Dyer.

The same account says Lucille Armstrong unveiled the statue in the new park on April 15, 1980, during the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival. Congo Square Connection, describing the Roots of Music Cultural Sculpture Garden, calls the Catlett figure 12 feet and says more than a thousand donations from 26 countries paid for it. The two opened pages do not agree on the height. Catlett also made the park's Mahalia Jackson sculpture, dedicated April 28, 2010.

paragraphs: Louisiana Revised Statute 33:9356, enacted as Acts 2005, No. 288, sets a nine-member board for the Veterans' Memorial District of Ward 10 of Lafourche Parish. Members must live in the ward, and at least six must be honorably discharged veterans. Six seats come from three local posts: Gros Guidry VFW Post 8538 in Larose, Delvin Adams American Legion Post 315 in Galliano, and Anthony N. Griffin American Legion Post 259 in Golden Meadow. A 2023 legislative audit lists the district contact as 16937 Hwy 3235, Cut Off, LA 70345.

The Lafourche Gazette, writing in December 2022, describes Veterans Memorial Park in Galliano: a wall with more than 4,000 names, a Field of Tears for 49 Ward 10 residents killed in battle, and free rides to VA appointments for about 220 veterans that year. The parish tourism bureau lists the South Lafourche Veterans Memorial at the same Cut Off highway address, with landscaped grounds, a gazebo, a reflection pool, and a 900-square-foot meeting room. It calls the site one of the largest U.S. memorials with a granite wall dedicated to Vietnam veterans.

title: Ronald Reagan Statue in Covington
description: A bronze Ronald Reagan, smiling and saluting, stands at Covington's Tammany Trace Trailhead. It was placed there in June 2008.
subtitle: Bronze salute at the Tammany Trace trailhead
lede: A bronze Ronald Reagan, titled An American Hero, stands smiling and saluting at Covington's Tammany Trace Trailhead. NOLA.com and Roadside America both treat it as the largest Reagan figure, and they print different heights.
paragraphs: A June 25, 2025, NOLA.com article says a 9-foot, 1,300-pound bronze of Ronald Reagan has stood for years at the Tammany Trace Trailhead and is reportedly the world's tallest, two feet taller than statues in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda and Budapest. A photo caption in the same article says a crane set a 9-foot-4-inch bronze on June 25, 2008. Roadside America says Reagan stands almost 10 feet tall, one and a half times life size, on a six-foot pedestal, in a business suit with his right arm raised in a salute. The opened pages do not agree on a single height.

Reagan never visited Covington as president. The memorial came from oilman Patrick F. Taylor, a friend of Reagan. NOLA.com says Taylor died in November 2004, before the project was finished, and that the Patrick F. Taylor Foundation later paid for it. Sculptor Patrick Miller, called a Bedico artist in the article and a Ponchatoula artist in the caption, finished the statue in March 2007 for $110,000. It was placed at the trailhead in June 2008 and looks over a small amphitheater. Roadside America puts it at the southwest corner of North New Hampshire and East Lockwood streets.

paragraphs: Oscoda Township says Furtaw Field, in downtown Oscoda on US-23, is a 3.3-acre property used as a town gathering spot. It boasts a Paul Bunyan statue and is used for community events. Destination Oscoda lists the field at 415 N. Lake Street, Oscoda, MI 48750, just off US-23, and names Paul Bunyan Days and Oscoda Rockfest. Rockfest has been held there since 2019, and its proceeds support the Veteran Memorial Park Fund.

paragraphs: Roadside America says a rock with a plaque was unveiled in 2005 for Stevie Wonder, born Stevland Hardaway Judkins in Saginaw in 1950. paragraphs: Lincoln City's public-art inventory lists Abraham Lincoln on Horseback by Anna Hyatt Huntington, installed in 1965 and dedicated on October 9, 1965, with Governor Hatfield present, at the start of the 20 Miracle Miles Autumn Festival of the Arts. It stands at the corner of Northeast 22nd Street and Northeast Quay Place, near Kirtsis Park. The city records a donation by Huntington on behalf of the school children of the Oregon Territory. Ownership transferred to Lincoln City on November 12, 1965, with an agreement that the city maintain the statue and park and not change the city's name. The statue was damaged on the way from the East Coast, and the city hired sculptor James Hansen to restore it.

The Oregon Encyclopedia says the five towns incorporated as Lincoln City on March 3, 1965, and that in that year Huntington donated a bronze of Abraham Lincoln, dedicated by Hatfield. Country Traveler describes a 14-foot bronze, Lincoln on the Prairie, one of three castings, showing a beardless Lincoln reading on a grazing horse. It says the work recalls his decision not to become governor of the Oregon Territory, and that the move west broke two hooves, a rein, and the horse's nose, repaired by Vancouver sculptor James Lee Hansen. Roadside America places the reading figure on 22nd Street and Quay Place, about a block or two off Highway 101, facing north.
